name: Mankon
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mfonyam, Joseph Ngwa. 1989. Tone in orthography: the case of Bafut and related languages. These de Doctorat d'Etat, Universite de Yaounde. xvi+686 pp. (open copy: MPG PuRe, hdl 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7EEE-C; also CORE 210667367)
catalog_locator: Chapter Twenty-two 'Mankon Tone', sec. 22.5 (review of Leroy 1977), pp. 393-395; first sentence spans bottom of p. 393 to top of p. 394, second sentence is on p. 395 (not p. 394 as both checks said). pp. 390-392 rendered
catalog_quote: Although in some of the languages where extra H tone exists, its realization is related to a falling tone, its realization in Mankon, by Leroy's description, is different or rather unique. Faraclas (1984:14), who recognizes a similar tone in Obolo, says that the extra H tone in Obolo comes from two sources: "lexically it is derived from a falling tone, while grammatically, it has developed as the result of stress patterns in the language." In Mankon we find that Leroy's super high tone does not originate from a falling tone neither can it be said to have developed from any kind of stress pattern since Mankon does not seem to be a stress accent language. [...] Following what has been said above about the source of extra high in the other languages, we see that its realization in Mankon, as described by Leroy, is different. In Mankon Leroy's super high tone is not related to intonation nor is it limited to grammatical particles. It is obvious that this tone is not related to any stress pattern in Mankon either.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mankon is a tone language (H/L with downstep, upstep, floating tones); it is judged not to be a stress-accent language, and no word-stress position is stated in any opened source. Loanwords map English primary stress onto H tone (Swiri 1998). If any prominence exists it is, per a family-level survey (Anderson 2001), predictable on the first root syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The statement is hedged ('does not seem to be'). Anderson 2001 (family level) reports predictable root-initial prominence, which is not contradictory if that prominence is non-contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in a discussion of Leroy's (1977) Mankon tone rules (super-high tone); no word forms or placement rule given. Supporting: Swiri 1998 p. 73 calls Mankon a tone language in which English primary-stressed syllables are borrowed as H tone. Family-level counterpoint: Anderson 2001 p. 47 says Eastern Grassfields (incl. Ngemba/Mankon) nouns and verbs carry predictable amplitude prominence on the first root syllable (Ngiemboon examples).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement concerns Mankon proper (Glottolog dialect mank1253, the reference lect of ngem1255) as described by Leroy 1977. Swiri 1998 also describes Mankon; Ngum 1997 describes the Njong dialect (njon1238). Anderson 2001 is a family-level claim for Eastern Grassfields that lists 'Ngemba (Bafut, Mankon..)' in scope but draws its examples from Ngiemboon (ngie1240), so it is not a Mankon statement. Mfonyam 1989 is a Bafut (bafu1246) thesis whose author also gathered Mankon, Nkwen and Bambili tone data.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2.2 'Harmonisation of prosody' p. 73 (p. 82, verified on page scan): 'The Mankon language being an African language is no exception for being a tone language. Loan-words from these stress-timed languages are compelled to bear tones. H tones are marked where syllables bearing primary stress are borrowed. The unstressed syllable bears L or M tones.' Sec. 1.5 Tones pp. 19-20 (H, L, HL, LH); no native stress statement.
